analysis.one_liner: Lets independent musicians and songwriters collectively negotiate licensing rates with major streaming platforms and AI music companies.
analysis.headline: The bill to let independent musicians bargain together sits untouched in the House Judiciary Committee, with 4 cosponsors and no action since its June 2026 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates an antitrust safe harbor for independent musicians, songwriters, producers, and small record labels — those earning under $1 million a year in licensing revenue — to negotiate as a group with dominant online music platforms, defined as music services with over $100 million in annual music revenue, and with companies developing generative AI. Under current antitrust law, small creators coordinating on licensing terms could be prosecuted as a price-fixing cartel; this bill exempts that coordination when it is directed at negotiating with those large platforms. If creators choose, they may collectively refuse to license their music to a platform or to a generative AI company, giving them the same leverage large labels get from their catalog size.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent music creator owners: self-releasing musicians, songwriters, producers, mixers, and engineers who own their copyrights and market their own work. The bill's own findings describe them as lacking the economic, legal, and political resources to negotiate with dominant platforms, which currently dictate take-it-or-leave-it terms — and profit from unlicensed uploads if creators refuse. Group negotiation would let them bargain for licensing rates closer to market value and, if bargaining fails, withdraw their catalogs together. Small record labels and music publishers under the size threshold can join the same coordination.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Independent musicians, songwriters, and small labels

how_it_helps.text: Exempts independent music creator owners — those owning sound recording or musical work copyrights with under $1 million in annual licensing revenue, or qualifying as small businesses — from antitrust liability for agreeing to collectively negotiate or collectively refuse to license to dominant platforms or generative AI companies. [S2]

Applies to platforms with more than $100 million in annual music-related revenue that are not covered by existing statutory licenses, directly targeting large streaming and distribution services that the bill says currently dictate licensing prices to small creators and profit from unlicensed uploads. [S2]

Conditions the safe harbor on nondiscrimination among similarly situated independent creators and limits coordination to what is reasonably necessary for bargaining with dominant platforms, with a rule of construction that otherwise preserves the antitrust laws. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Dominant online music platforms — large streaming and distribution services — would face organized bargaining from small creators and potentially coordinated withdrawal of catalogs, raising their royalty costs and likely cutting into margins or, at the margin, subscription prices. Companies developing or deploying generative AI that train on or license recorded music would face the possibility of coordinated refusals from independent creators, restricting their access to training and licensing material.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large streaming platforms and generative AI music companies

drawbacks.text: Collective negotiation could raise platform royalty costs that are partly passed to consumers as higher subscription or service prices, a cost the bill does not quantify. [S2]

Coordinated refusal to license may chill development and deployment of generative AI companies' lawful uses of recorded music, and the bill does not resolve the underlying copyright disputes about AI training that it partially leverages. [S2]

The bill addresses only the power imbalance in bargaining: it does not change the notice-and-takedown system under the Digital Millennium Copyright Act or require higher statutory royalty rates, so independent creators' actual gains depend on how much leverage group action can build. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, well-documented imbalance: small creators must individually accept terms from platforms that profit from unlicensed use, while a collective bargaining exemption is the standard remedy labor uses against employer power. The costs — somewhat higher royalty expenses for platforms and possible friction for AI music developers — are real but modest and fall on concentrated interests, with some risk of pass-through to consumers. The main design limitation is that a safe harbor grants bargaining rights, not guaranteed outcomes; it depends on enough small creators organizing for the leverage to matter.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on June 10, 2026 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has received no hearing, markup, or floor action so far in the Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Ross introduced the bill on June 10, 2026 with three original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary. [S4]
The bill has 4 cosponsors in total, all House Democrats; no Republicans have joined. [S3]

The bill text sets the eligibility thresholds that determine who may bargain together: creators with under $1 million in annual licensing revenue (or small-business status) versus platforms with more than $100 million in annual music revenue. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dominant streaming platforms and generative AI companies benefit from the bill not moving, since they avoid organized small-creator bargaining. Working musicians gain nothing yet; the outcome preserves the status quo in which platforms set terms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large streaming platforms and AI music companies

for.name: Deborah Ross
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 9253 and carried it to committee referral

for.name: Steve Cohen, Lloyd Doggett, and Daniel Goldman
for.role: Original cosponsors; House Democrats from Tennessee, Texas, and New York
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, bringing the bill's total support to 4 House Democrats

against.name: Jim Jordan
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the time since referral, leaving it without committee action

sides.party_line_note: All 4 cosponsors are House Democrats, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee has taken no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Dominant online music streaming and distribution platforms
industries.note: Organized bargaining and possible coordinated catalog withdrawal from small creators would raise the royalty costs these services now set largely unilaterally; the platforms' current advantage in dictating below-market terms comes directly at working musicians' expense. Consumers may see modest price pass-through.

industries.industry: Independent music creator owners (musicians, songwriters, producers, small labels)
industries.note: The people this class covers are working creators earning under $1 million in licensing revenue; group negotiation gives them the leverage a large catalog owner gets from size, aimed at raising what platforms pay for their work.

The bill lets independent creators collectively refuse to license to AI companies, restricting access to training and licensing material these firms want; the safe harbor is part of the broader fight over AI's use of copyrighted music.

Major labels are excluded from the safe harbor's coordinated negotiations, which involve only independent creator owners; they lose no existing rights but face no new burden either, though stronger independent negotiating could slightly erode the label market power the bill's findings describe.

analysis.trajectory: With only 4 cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action months after referral, this bill is likely to die in the House Judiciary Committee when the 119th Congress ends, as similar collective-negotiation proposals for musicians have in prior Congresses. Path to the floor would require the committee chair to schedule a markup or a discharge petition gathering 218 signatures, neither of which has any visible support.
